title: Deterministic linear-time static dictionaries
formal: Is the following proposition true? For every fixed integer \(d\ge 1\) there are uniform deterministic construction and query programs \(A_{d},Q_{d}\) and a constant \(C_{d}\ge 1\) such that, for every \(n\ge 2\), every word length \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil \le w\le d\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\), and every n-record input with distinct w-bit integer keys and w-bit values, \(A_{d}\) builds a static dictionary in at most \(C_{d} n\) operations and \(C_{d} n\) words of total space, and \(Q_{d}\) answers every membership-and-value query in at most \(C_{d}\) operations.
why: Exact constant-time lookup is a basic component of many larger data structures. The unresolved cost is obtaining the representation deterministically in optimal time, so a resolution would settle whether randomness is essential to this combination of construction, storage and lookup guarantees.
status_note: The primary dictionary results, later applications and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No complete resolution of the specified logarithmic-word deterministic construction target was found. The accessible 2025 draft Slightly more practical deterministic static dictionaries was also inspected; it contains unfinished statements and does not claim the required linear construction, so it is not used to certify a new bound.
review_note: User-approved research proposal, imported as a short draft. Its importance was assessed editorially; the full research-card standard has not yet been completed.

progress.text: Pagh gives deterministic \(O(n \log  n)\) construction with linear space and constant lookup for \(w=O(\log  n)\); the paper contrasts this with randomized expected linear construction.
Ružić brings deterministic construction within a log log n factor of sorting time while retaining linear space and constant lookup.
The internal-pattern-matching journal paper uses general deterministic dictionaries with \(O(m(\log  \log  m)^{2})\) construction and distinguishes restricted small instances.
Kosolobov’s CPM paper records a construction slowdown when replacing randomized dictionaries in a compressed index. This is an application, not a solution of the present static target.

importance.reason: A foundational derandomization question for exact lookup: linear construction, linear storage and constant worst-case queries would give many algorithms an optimal deterministic dictionary primitive. The 2024 and 2026 string-indexing applications show concrete dependencies on dictionary construction costs.

category_assignment.reason: User-approved Data structures split, 2026-09-11: The target is construction and lookup performance of a static dictionary, a basic data-structure primitive.

sentences: A static dictionary stores distinct integer keys together with associated values and supports exact membership queries.
The question asks for deterministic linear-time construction, linear space, and constant worst-case query time on the stated word RAM.
All preprocessing work must be included in the construction bound.
Random hashing motivates the desired efficiency but does not itself provide a deterministic construction.
A solution would give other algorithms a dependable dictionary primitive without making their preprocessing randomized or increasing their asymptotic running time.

upgraded_from.title: Deterministic linear-time construction of static dictionaries

definitions: The universe is \(U_{w}\)={\(0,\ldots ,2\)ʷ−1}. An input is a list of n pairs \((x_{i},v_{i})\in U_{w}\times U_{w}\) with pairwise distinct \(x_{i}\) and arbitrary \(v_{i}\); the input order is unrestricted. On query \(q\in U_{w}\) the output is \((1,v_{i})\) if \(q=x_{i}\) and \((0,0)\) if q is absent. The stored set and values do not change after construction. The machine is a sequential word RAM with w-bit registers and cells. The primitive unit-cost instructions are memory reads and writes, copies, comparisons, conditional branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication returning the full product in two words, integer quotient and remainder of two words with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least w returns zero; otherwise shifted-out bits are discarded. Addresses may occupy a fixed number of words, and all operations computing them are charged. Programs have finitely many instructions and constants, may receive n and w, and contain no input-size or word-size advice, random instruction, free table or special hashing primitive. Every table, parameter computation, memory initialization and output write performed by construction counts toward its time; input storage, the resulting dictionary and temporary storage count toward its space. Query reads the constructed representation and may use temporary workspace, with every operation charged; all retained information about the input is in the counted representation. The query must be correct on every q, including absent keys. Programs and constants may depend on d but not on n, w, the input or query. This spells out the saved \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) convention as a claim for every fixed polynomial-size universe; Pagh’s broader arbitrary-word-length formulation is not asserted equivalent here.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition with deterministic algorithms meeting all three bounds for every fixed d, or disprove it for at least one fixed d. The negation says that no pair of admissible correct programs has simultaneously linear worst-case construction time, linear total space and constant worst-case query time for all inputs in that word-length range. Failure of a particular hash family, an average-input lower bound, or a lower bound in a comparison-only model is not that negation.

context_blocks.text: A dictionary is an exact lookup table for a sparse set of keys. For example, records \((12,5), (47,9)\) and \((103,2)\) require the answers 9 on key 47 and absent on key 48. The values need not be unique. The problem is to prepare a representation in time proportional to the number of records and then answer every lookup in a bounded number of machine steps, regardless of whether the key is present.

Direct addressing uses the key itself as an array index. This achieves constant lookup time, but an array for a universe of \(n^{2}\) possible keys occupies \(n^{2}\) cells even if only n keys are present. Such space is outside the target. At the opposite extreme, keeping the keys in sorted order uses linear space but ordinary binary search needs logarithmically many comparisons. These examples show why construction, storage and query time must be required simultaneously.

Randomized perfect hashing already gives linear expected construction time, linear storage and constant worst-case lookup time. The randomness concerns finding a suitable representation during construction; once a valid dictionary has been built, lookup can be exact and have a worst-case bound. Thus the open issue is not whether every query can avoid probabilistic errors, but whether the construction time can be bounded linearly without any random choices.

Pagh obtained deterministic \(O(n \log  n)\) construction for logarithmic-size words. Ružić subsequently related construction cost to integer sorting with only a log log n overhead. The latter is a much smaller overhead, but it still grows with n. The source question asks for its complete removal while retaining the other two guarantees. A representation whose existence is known but whose parameters take longer to find does not meet the construction requirement.

The dependence on word length matters even when keys occupy one machine word. Here a fixed polynomial-size universe is intended: the constant relating w to log n is fixed before the inputs vary. Constants in the guarantees may depend on that fixed bound. This is the logarithmic-word version already selected for this card; it does not silently claim a solution for word lengths growing faster than log n.

Uniformity also matters. Earlier dictionary results sometimes supplied word-size-dependent constants at no construction cost. The present formulation charges for computing every table and parameter that is not part of a fixed program. A one-time computation on a particular physical machine cannot disappear from an asymptotic bound that covers arbitrarily large inputs.

The dependency remains visible in modern applications. The 2024 internal-pattern-matching paper uses constant-time deterministic dictionaries with a general \(O(m(\log  \log  m)^{2})\) construction bound for a dictionary of size m, and treats very small dictionaries separately. The surrounding text length can be much larger than m, so that application must not be read as fixing word length to \(\Theta (\log  m)\). Kosolobov’s 2026 compressed index likewise records a slowdown when dictionary randomness is removed.

These applications explain the scientific stakes: a basic lookup operation can determine whether a larger construction remains deterministic within its intended time bound. The 2026 index is evidence that the issue remains useful, rather than a theorem resolving this static linear-construction question.
